content: CD69, also known as Cluster of Differentiation 69, is a human transmembrane C-type lectin protein encoded by the CD69 gene. It serves as an early activation marker expressed in hematopoietic stem cells, T cells, and various other immune cell types. CD69 plays a role in T cell differentiation and lymphocyte retention within lymphoid organs. Function The activation of T lymphocytes and Natural Killer (NK) cells, both in vivo and in vitro, induces the expression of CD69. This protein is involved in immune cell signaling and regulation. Structure and Ligands The CD69 gene is located in the NK gene complex on chromosome 6 in mice and chromosome 12 in humans. Activation signaling pathways in lymphocytes, NK cells, dendritic cells, and other cell types upregulate transcription factors such as NF-κB, ERG-1 (Erythroblast Transformation-Specific Related Gene-1), and AP-1 (Activator Protein-1), which promote the transcription of the CD69 gene. The CD69 protein undergoes post-translational modifications, including differential glycosylation, resulting in either a 28 kDa or 32 kDa peptide. These peptides randomly combine to form a homodimer linked by a disulfide bond. The CD69 protein contains a C-type lectin domain (CTLD) that binds ligands, a transmembrane domain, and a cytoplasmic tail that transduces signals to the cell interior. Unlike typical CTLDs, CD69 lacks the characteristic calcium-binding residues, suggesting it may bind proteins rather than carbohydrates. CD69 has been shown to bind Galectin-1 (Gal-1), a carbohydrate-binding protein found on some dendritic cells and macrophages, as well as Myosin Light Chain 9/12 (Myl9/12). Other ligands remain unidentified, but ligand binding is known to initiate the JAK/STAT signaling pathway and the mTOR/HIF1-α pathway. CD69 also interacts with and mediates S1P and LAT1 receptors, influencing lymphocyte egress from lymphoid organs and other immune responses. Further research is needed to fully characterize CD69-ligand interactions and its intracellular signaling mechanisms. T Cell Differentiation CD69 expression is associated with regulatory T cells (Tregs), memory T cells, and Bcl6loCD69hi light zone germinal center B cell plasmablast precursors. Treg precursors exit the thymus expressing CD69 and complete their differentiation into Tregs in peripheral tissues upon encountering antigens and cytokines such as IL-2. Through the JAK/STAT signaling pathway, CD69 activation induces the production of TGF-β and IL-2, which contribute to Treg differentiation. Additionally, CD69 is upregulated by NF-κB signaling during the onset of an immune response. A prolonged immune response is maintained by the non-canonical NF-κB pathway, which is also associated with Treg differentiation. CD69 is a common marker of precursor and mature tissue-resident memory T cells (TRMs) localized in peripheral tissues. TGF-β is also responsible for TRM development, promoting their differentiation in a manner similar to Tregs. Lymphocyte Migration Most lymphocytes express sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) receptors (S1P1-5), which are G protein-coupled receptors located in the cell membrane that bind the ligand sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P). S1P is a sphingolipid metabolite abundant in the bloodstream. Upon binding to S1P1, it promotes lymphocyte egress from lymphoid organs, allowing them to travel to affected tissues. When a T cell is activated in a lymphoid organ through cytokine and TCR signaling, CD69 is expressed and forms a complex with S1P1 (but not S1P3 or S1P5). This association depends on the interaction between the CD69 transmembrane domain and helix-4 of S1P1. Following the formation of this complex, S1P1 is internalized and degraded within the cell, inhibiting its ability to bind S1P and initiate downstream signaling. This results in temporary lymphocyte retention in lymphoid organs. It is hypothesized that lymphocyte retention in lymph nodes increases the likelihood of successful lymphocyte activation, particularly if the initial activation signal was weak. Similarly, CD69 expression in thymocytes following positive selection may ensure that T cells fully mature in the thymus before entering circulation. Some research suggests that S1P1 and CD69 co-regulate each other. When CD69 is more abundant, it leads to the removal of S1P1 from the membrane. Conversely, if S1P1 is more abundant than CD69, as in mature T cells, CD69 membrane localization is reduced. In this way, the regulation of CD69 and S1P1 expression and localization jointly impacts lymphocyte egress and migration.
